Living Things and Their Homes

What do living things need, and how do homes and helpers support them?

Plants and animals need certain things, and their homes give them what they need. You will find out what living things need to survive, how habitats supply food, water, shelter and space, how living things change the places they live, and how people can help.

In this lesson

  1. Plants and animals have needs
  2. Homes meet needs
  3. Living things change your environment
  4. People can reduce harm
  5. Try it at home
  6. Check yourself
  7. Play: Habitat Helper

You did this before / what is new. You noticed sunlight and water in Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe; now you connect needs to homes, see how living things change places, and take one real helper action.

Concept 1

Plants and animals have needs

Plants and animals need things such as water, air, food, sunlight, and space to survive.

Analogy

Think of a needs list, like a shopping list. Everyone has a list of things they must get to stay alive.

  • A plant’s list: water, sunlight, air, space.
  • An animal’s list: food, water, air, space.

The lists are not the same, but each living thing needs everything on its own list.

“Plants need water and sunlight. Animals need food, water, and air.”

Try it

Living things need water to live; rocks and toys do not.

Sort living things from nonliving things, then match each one’s needs.

Ask of each card: “Does it need water?”

Cards to sort:

  • Bean plant
  • Deer
  • Fish
  • Robin
  • Rock
  • Sand
  • Toy truck

Needs cards to match: water, sunlight, air, food, space.

“Does it need water?”

Data

Needs chart for a bean plant and a deer.

“Bean plant: water, sunlight, air, space. Deer: food, water, air, space.”

Real world

Michigan robins eat worms, drink water, and need safe places.

“Robins need food and water.”

Concept 2

Homes meet needs

A habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space; different habitats have different living things.

Diagram

Pond, forest, and sand dune.

“A pond gives fish water.”

Try it

Sort these Michigan living things into the pond, forest, or sand dune:

  • Frog: pond
  • Bluegill: pond
  • Cattail: pond
  • White-tailed deer: forest
  • Sugar maple: forest
  • American beach grass: sand dune
  • Gull: sand dune

Where does the frog live?

“Where does the frog live?”

Try it

Guess first: What does your animal need in its home? Plan it first.

What you need:

  • Clay or play dough
  • Paper
  • Crayons
  • Blue paper for water
  • A small tray (about 20 by 30 centimeters, or 8 by 12 inches)

Do: Pick one animal, such as a frog, deer, or fish. Make its home on the tray. Add blue paper for water, paper trees or grass for shelter, and little clay bits for food. Put the animal in.

Look for: Check the model against the needs list: does it have water, food, shelter, and space?

What it shows: A habitat is the place that meets an animal’s needs. If one need is missing, the home does not work.

“My model has water, shelter, and food.”

Data

Count different living things in habitat pictures.

“Forest had 6 kinds.”

Do: Look at one habitat picture at a time with a grown-up. Count each different kind of living thing (a kind is one sort, like deer or trees, no matter how many there are). Write the number. “Forest had 6 kinds” is an example; your count may be different.

  • Pond picture: ___ kinds
  • Forest picture: ___ kinds
  • Sand dune picture: ___ kinds

Which habitat had the most kinds?

Real world

Great Lakes shores have water, sand, plants, birds, and insects.

“The shore is a home.”

Concept 3

Living things change your environment

Your environment is everything around a living thing, like its water, soil, plants, and air.

Living things change the places around them to meet needs.

Diagram

A dam is a wall that blocks the water in a stream.

Beaver dam blocking a stream.

“Beavers make dams.”

Try it

Look at the evidence cards:

  • Beaver dam
  • Worm tunnels
  • Bird nest
  • Dog digging
  • Squirrel with acorns

“Did a living thing change this place?”

Data

An argument here means a claim backed by evidence.

Our class argument chart has four parts: Place, Changed?, Evidence, and Who changed it.

  • Sample: Place: stream. Changed? Yes. Evidence: dam of sticks. Who changed it: beaver.

Fill in the same four parts for the soil and for the tree.

“I see tunnels. A worm changed the soil.”

Concept 4

People can reduce harm

People can make choices that help local land, water, air, and living things.

Analogy

We can be habitat helpers. Your two hands are like helper hands for a place. Picking up litter helps animals stay safe. Planting a native flower gives bees food.

Each small action is one helping hand for the land, water, air, or living things.

“We can be habitat helpers.”

Try it

Guess first: How many pieces of litter will we find in the schoolyard? Guess a number.

What you need for the litter pick:

  • An adult
  • Gloves
  • A bag
  • A camera or paper to draw on

What you need for planting:

  • A native flower plant
  • A small pot or garden spot
  • A watering can

Do: Take a “before” photo or drawing of the spot. Then, with an adult, pick up the litter into the bag and count the pieces (do not touch sharp things). Or plant the native flower and water it. Take an “after” photo or drawing.

Look for: Compare before and after. Was there less litter? How many pieces did we pick up? What helped?

What it shows: Real actions change a real place, and the pictures are our evidence.

Safety: Always wear gloves, never touch sharp objects, and wash hands after.

“We pick up litter. We take a before photo and an after photo.”

Data

Before/after photo or tally chart.

“Before: 10 litter pieces. After: 0.”

Sample numbers: before 10 pieces, after 0 pieces. Your class’s numbers may be different.

Real world

Native flowers help bees and butterflies.

“Native flowers help bees.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Habitat Helper Action. A pollinator is an animal, like a bee or butterfly, that carries pollen from flower to flower. Students choose a local habitat problem, such as litter near the schoolyard or lack of pollinator plants. They carry out one real action: a supervised litter pick with before/after photos or planting a native flower. They draw a habitat model and say how their action helps land, water, air, or living things.

Try it

What you need

  • Michigan plant and animal pictures
  • Bean plant or bean plant photo
  • Paper
  • Crayons
  • Clay or play dough
  • Blue paper for water
  • Evidence cards
  • Tape
  • Gloves for the litter pick
  • Camera or drawing sheet for before and after evidence

Safety: Wash hands after soil, sand, plants, or outdoor litter work. Adults help with litter pickup; do not touch sharp objects. No coin cells or magnets are needed.

Try it

What you do

1. Needs (15 minutes). Use the card sort above, then make a needs chart for a bean plant and a deer.

2. Habitat model (20 minutes). Build a model for one animal with water, food, and shelter. Check it against the needs list.

3. Evidence cards (10 minutes). Sort the cards to argue how a living thing changed a place.

4. Helper action (30 minutes, with an adult). Do one real action: a supervised litter pick with before and after photos, or plant a native flower.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but it is better to collect your own when you can.

If you cannot grow or observe a bean plant, use this data:

  • Bean plant needs: water, sunlight, air, and space.
  • Deer needs: food, water, air, and space.
  • Habitat picture counts: pond 4 kinds (bluegill, frog, cattail, water lily); forest 6 kinds (white-tailed deer, sugar maple, fern, squirrel, robin, trillium); sand dune 3 kinds (American beach grass, gull, beetle).
  • Evidence cards: beaver dam, worm tunnels, bird nest, squirrel with acorns, dog digging.
  • Before and after sample: litter pieces before 10, after 0.

What did you learn?

Words to know

living thing
a plant, animal, or other thing that is alive.
need
something required to live or grow.
habitat
home that gives needs.
shelter
a safe place to live.
environment
the place around a living thing.
change
make something different.
reduce
make less.
native
naturally from a place.
evidence
what we see that helps answer a question.
survive
stay alive.
pollen
yellow dust from flowers.
nectar
sweet juice from flowers.
pollinator
an animal that carries pollen from flower to flower.
dam
a wall that blocks water in a stream.
dune
a hill of sand made by wind and water.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes (150 minutes in all). The four hands-on steps add up to 75 minutes of that.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • Misconception: “Plants eat soil.” Correct: plants need water, light, and air; soil holds the plant in place and gives it water and minerals.
  • Misconception: “Plants need only dirt.” Correct: plants also need water, sunlight, air, and space.
  • Misconception: “A habitat is only where an animal sleeps.” Correct: a habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space.
  • Misconception: “Living things do not change their environment.” Correct: organisms can change their surroundings.
  • Misconception: “Only people change the environment.” Correct: animals and plants can change environments too.
  • Misconception: “People cannot help nature.” Correct: local actions can reduce harm.
  • Misconception: “Litter does not harm habitats.” Correct: litter can harm land, water, and living things.

Limits and cautions:

  • The local-action standard is only partly covered unless students complete one real local action with evidence.
  • Litter picks need adult supervision, gloves, and permission. Do not touch sharp objects.
  • If planting is not possible, use a photo dataset and a classroom “before/after” simulation, but note that real action gives the strongest evidence.
  • This unit does not cover external parts, biomimicry, parent-offspring behavior, or young resembling parents; those belong in the Parts, Parents, and Young and Plants, Animals, and Habitats units.
  • Food needs are simplified; ecosystems are more complex and are developed later in Energy and Matter in Ecosystems.

Connections:

  • Builds on: Science Noticing and Asking if taught; Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe for sunlight and water.
  • Builds toward: Parts, Parents, and Young; Plants, Animals, and Habitats; Life Cycles and Traits; Survival, Fossils, and Change; Energy and Matter in Ecosystems; Cells; Classifying Life; Ecosystems & Food Webs; and Photosynthesis & Matter Cycling.
